extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers of reflective/personal essays; students of Montaigne and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for composing and reading personal, philosophical essays that emphasize modesty, skepticism, plain speech, and restraint in learning and ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject ambition and thirst for renown
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let us reject ambition; let us disdain that thirst of honour and renown, so low and mendicant, that it makes us beg it of all sorts of people.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek honour by obsequious or abject means; prefer natural, fitting pleasures to grandeur. Ambition that courts cheap praise is dishonourable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer silent, unostentatious good deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: “All things truly seem more laudable to me that are performed without ostentation, and without the testimony of the people.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts that ‘slip from the hand’ negligently and are later discovered have greater grace; ostentation diminishes moral worth. Avoid performing good primarily for public applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renown requires novelty and difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: “Renown does not follow all good deeds, if novelty and difficulty be not conjoined.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every useful or virtuous action deserves high praise—rarity and challenge contribute to deserved fame. Trivial public works may be praised by monuments but not by discerning minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbearance can be as generous as action
rubrics_metrics.description: “To forbear doing is often as generous as to do; but ‘tis less in the light.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes refraining from action is morally valuable; such virtues are quieter and less likely to be celebrated but are genuinely praiseworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not desire troubles to showcase your skill
rubrics_metrics.description: “Is there any who desires to be sick, that he may see his physician at work?... I have never been of that wicked humour... to desire that troubles and disorders in this city should elevate and honour my government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should not hope for crises in order to display competence. It is dishonourable to wish for others’ misfortune for personal glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underpromise rather than overpromise
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am apt to promise something less than what I am able to do, and than what I hope to make good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage expectations by promising less than your capacity; this reduces resentment and leaves room for favorable judgment of your performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask whether something is true before asking how it is done
rubrics_metrics.description: “They commonly begin thus: ‘How is such a thing done?’ Whereas they should say, ‘Is such a thing done?’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on establishing the fact/existence of a claim before investigating causes. Reason easily invents causes; confirm the effect first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend judgment; prefer doubt for hard-to-prove matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Echoing St. Augustine: “’tis better to lean towards doubt than assurance, in things hard to prove and dangerous to believe.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evidence is weak or matters are extraordinary, withhold assent. Use cautious, provisional belief rather than dogmatic assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use qualifying language; avoid dogmatic affirmations
rubrics_metrics.description: “I love these words which mollify and moderate the temerity of our propositions: ‘peradventure; in some sort; some; ‘tis said, I think,’ and the like.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a habit of modest, tentative phrasing (perhaps, I think, it may be) especially in teaching or inquiry; train learners to inquire rather than to assert prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of miracles and supernatural claims without extraordinary proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne argues that human witnesses are unreliable for supernatural effects and that such claims should be believed only when ‘authorised by a supernatural approbation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural explanations where possible; require very strong, exceptional evidence (or divine authorization) before accepting supernatural accounts. Examples: miraculous travel, spirit possessions, witches—seek mundane causes first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize how reports are embellished in transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: “The particular error first makes the public error, and afterwards, in turn, the public error makes the particular one... so that the remotest witness knows more about it than those who were nearest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hearsay and successive testimony with suspicion: people naturally add to and nourish rumours. The proliferation of believers is not a reliable test of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority, antiquity, and numbers are not proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: “For my part, what I should not believe from one, I should not believe from a hundred and one: and I do not judge opinions by years.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take numbers of witnesses, long standing, or age of opinion as decisive evidence. Critically evaluate the quality of reasons, not mere quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat confessions and witness testimony as fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: Noting that some have confessed to murders of persons later found living, Montaigne warns against relying blindly on personal confessions and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate alternative, natural explanations (madness, error, imposture) before rendering severe judgments; legal/punitive measures require clear, careful proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit and confess ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Neither am I ashamed... to confess my ignorance of what I do not know.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honest admission of ignorance is a philosophical virtue and the appropriate posture for learners and inquirers; it preserves intellectual humility and opens space for true inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value simplicity and plainness over learned ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne praises Socrates’ simple, popular examples and argues that simplicity can produce the most vigorous and useful beliefs and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clarity, common examples, and natural expression over pompous or artificially elevated style; genuine wisdom often appears in ordinary speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict appetite for knowledge; beware overconsumption of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: “Its acquisition is far more hazardous than that of all other meat or drink... some [learning] only burden and overcharge the stomach, instead of nourishing; and, moreover, some that, under colour of curing, poison us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach study with moderation: excessive or indiscriminate reading can confuse or corrupt the mind. Consider vows of intellectual modesty and restraint when appropriate.
